steps.body: Fill a square in halves: first 1/2, then 1/4, then 1/8… forever. Each new piece fills exactly half of whatever gap remains — so the total climbs and climbs but **never passes 1**. Infinitely many additions, finite total. That's the strange, beautiful idea this chapter makes precise.

widget.prompt: 4 + 4r + 4r² + … Set the ratio so the forever-sum settles on exactly 8.
widget.successFeedback: r = 0.5, and the partial sums pile up against the ceiling at 8 without ever passing it. An infinite sum is not 'adding forever' — it is the height the partial sums close in on. Drag r toward 1 and watch the ceiling run away: that is divergence, and it is why |r| < 1 is not a technicality.
widget.lowFeedback: The ceiling is under 8 — the terms shrink too fast, so the pile stops short.
widget.highFeedback: The ceiling is over 8 — the terms shrink too slowly. As r approaches 1 the ceiling escapes altogether.

predict.prompt: As the common ratio moves closer to 1 from below, what happens to the infinite geometric sum?

options.label: Its finite limit grows and eventually escapes as r approaches 1
Its limit shrinks toward the first term
The limit stays fixed because the first term is fixed

predict.reveal: The limit is a/(1 − r). As r approaches 1, the denominator approaches zero, so the ceiling rises without bound.

explanation.prompt: Why does a geometric series converge only when |r| < 1?

options.label: Only then do the term magnitudes shrink to zero fast enough for the partial sums to approach a finite ceiling.
options.feedback: Exactly — convergence is visible in the shrinking terms and stabilizing partial sums.

options.label: Any infinite list converges because later terms become less important.
options.feedback: If |r| is at least 1, terms do not shrink to zero, so the partial sums cannot settle.

explanationVariants: Every partial sum equals 1 − 1/2ⁿ — always a hair below 1, climbing ever closer.
Each piece fills half the REMAINING gap, so the gap shrinks forever but never empties.

widget.prompt: As more and more pieces are added, the running total…

options.label: climbs toward 1 but never reaches or passes it
options.feedback: Exactly — the total is trapped: always rising, never arriving. We say it CONVERGES to 1.

options.label: eventually exceeds 1
options.feedback: Each new piece fills only HALF the remaining gap — the gap never empties, so 1 is never passed.

options.label: reaches exactly 1 after finitely many pieces
options.feedback: Every partial sum is 1 − 1/2ⁿ — always a hair short. Only the infinite limit IS 1.

options.label: grows without bound
options.feedback: The pieces shrink fast enough that the total stays trapped below 1 forever.

steps.body: When does an infinite geometric series settle like this? Exactly when **|r| < 1** — the ratio must shrink each term toward zero. Then the partial sums converge to a finite value. If |r| ≥ 1, the terms never fade and the running total either explodes or bounces forever: it **diverges**.

widget.prompt: Sort each ratio by the fate of its infinite series.

items.label: r = 1/3
items.feedback: |1/3| < 1 — terms shrink toward 0 and the total settles.

items.label: r = 2
items.feedback: Terms DOUBLE each step — the running total explodes past every bound.

items.label: r = −0.9
items.feedback: The sign makes it alternate, but the SIZE decides: |−0.9| < 1, so it settles.

items.label: r = 1
items.feedback: r = 1 repeats the same term forever: a + a + a + ⋯ climbs without end.

items.label: r = −3/2
items.feedback: |−3/2| > 1 — the swings GROW each step; the total never settles on anything.

widget.missFeedback: Judge by |r| alone: strictly less than 1 settles; 1 or more diverges.
widget.successFeedback: |r| < 1 is the whole story — the sign only decides whether the approach alternates.

explanationVariants: Only 100 + 50 + 25 + ⋯ has |r| < 1 (each term is HALF the last) — the rest grow or repeat forever.
Check r term-over-term: 1/2 settles; 2, 1, and 3 do not.

widget.prompt: Which infinite series settles to a finite total?

options.feedback: r = 1/2 — the terms halve toward 0 and the total converges (to 200, as you'll soon compute).
r = 2 — each term doubles, so the running total grows past every bound.
r = 1 — the terms never shrink, and adding 5 forever climbs without end.
r = 3 — tripling terms explode even faster than doubling ones.

steps.body: Why the strict rule? Shrinking terms alone don't guarantee a finite total — the famous sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ⋯ has fading terms yet grows forever. **Geometric** shrinking is special: each term is a fixed FRACTION of the last, so the leftovers vanish fast enough to trap the total.

widget.prompt: The partial sums of 0.3 + 0.03 + 0.003 + ⋯ climb toward:

options.feedback: Right — the running totals are 0.3, 0.33, 0.333, … building the repeating decimal 0.333…, which IS 1/3.
The sums never even reach 0.34 — each new term is a tenth of the last, far too small to push that high.
That reads the first term as 3 — it's 0.3, and the whole pile stays below 0.34.

options.label: no ceiling — it grows forever
options.feedback: r = 1/10 shrinks the terms geometrically — the total is trapped. Growth without bound needs |r| ≥ 1.

explanationVariants: Only |r| < 1 settles: |−0.99| = 0.99 < 1 qualifies — barely and slowly, but it converges.
1.01 and 1 fail the size test; −1 makes the partial sums flip between two values forever.

widget.prompt: For which r does 6 + 6r + 6r² + 6r³ + ⋯ settle to a finite total?

options.label: r = −0.99
options.feedback: |−0.99| < 1 — just barely. The approach is slow and swings sign, but it settles.

options.label: r = 1.01
options.feedback: |1.01| > 1 — the terms GROW a little each step, and any growth compounds without bound.

options.label: r = −1
options.feedback: The terms run 6, −6, 6, −6… so the partial sums flip 6, 0, 6, 0 forever — never settling on one value.

options.label: r = 1
options.feedback: 6 + 6 + 6 + ⋯ climbs forever — the terms never shrink.

hints: Apply the one test that matters: is |r| strictly less than 1?
1.01 and 1 fail immediately. Between −0.99 and −1, take absolute values.

takeaways: An infinite geometric series converges exactly when |r| < 1.
Partial sums climb toward a ceiling they never cross.
The sign of r sets alternation; the SIZE of r decides the fate.

concept.body: One series, one test. 40 + 20 + 10 + 5 + ⋯ has r = 1/2: every term is half the last, so the terms fade toward 0 and the running total gets trapped below a ceiling. |r| < 1 means SETTLES — that single check is the entire convergence story.

explanationVariants: Halving terms fade toward 0; the pile can't grow past its ceiling.
